title: The Price of Auditing a Firewall: Query Complexity of Black-Box Verification for Listed-Rule and Tree-Rule Policies
content: Firewalls are audited, reverse-engineered and tested by sending packets and observing whether they pass, yet the literature offers algorithms, not lower bounds. We formulate black-box firewall verification as a query-complexity problem in Angluin's exact-learning framework, with oracles matched to what auditors and attackers observe: action-only queries, identity queries (hit counters, and flow logs where they are exact) and witness packets from captured traffic. We prove that shadowed rules are invisible to every black-box observer; that without side information even a single-rule policy on the IPv4 5-tuple needs 2¹⁰⁴ − 1 probes; and that with one witness per rule and identity feedback the reconstruction cost is governed by the number of leaves m of the policy's minimal Tree-Rule — (m − 1)(log W + d) + 2m probes, in which the number d of header fields is only an additive term, against 2n·Σ log W_j + n for a disjoint list of n rules, where d multiplies the logarithm. A fixed certificate of 3m − 2 packets is complete against structural misconfigurations and Θ(log W) cheaper than reconstruction, and N traffic samples bound the expected reconstruction error by m/(eN). Exact simulations, a real iptables testbed and 16 production rule sets confirm the bounds and expose a dichotomy: policies with small canonical trees are 13–26× cheaper to audit as trees, whereas cross-product policies inflate the tree by up to 83×, making the query complexity of overlapping rule lists the central open problem.
